children.text: Cervical adjacent segment disease refers to the radiographic degeneration of the disc or facets at the caudal or cephalad segment adjacent to a previous cervical surgical fusion construct
Diagnosis can be made with plain radiographs of the cervical spine
Treatment consists of observation and medical management for patients with mild symptoms. Surgical management is indicated in patients that have failed conservative treatment
studies have estimated a **1.6-2.4% annual incidence of clinically relevant ASD**
there is a predicted 25.6% ASD rate at 10 years postoperatively for patients undergoing ACDF
patients <60 y/o are at increased risk
the lowest three segments of the subaxial spine are the most commonly affected (C4-5, C5-6, and C6-7)
unclear as to whether this level is more prone to the natural progression of spondylosis or sensitive to adjacent segment disease
**smoking is the strongest associated risk factor**
**<3 segments included in the fusion construct**
it is speculated that fewer remaining motion segments reduces the risk of adjacent segment degeneration
**C5-6 and C6-7 segments are adjacent to the fusion construct**
these are anatomically the most mobile segments of the cervical spine with the highest rates of degeneration

no decrease in risk with fusion vs. nonfusion procedures (i.e. posterior foraminotomy or anterior discectomy)
